summary: Defines the LIMITS extension for SMTP, submission, and LMTP, letting a server tell a client what limits it will apply during the session. The client can then adapt. It also defines a registry of limits.

eli5.summary: A mail server tells you the rules before you start, like how many letters you can send, so you do not break them.

questions: how does a server advertise smtp limits
what is the smtp limits extension
how does a server tell clients its smtp limits
subtitle: How a mail server tells a client its limits up front, in the reply to EHLO, so the client stops tripping over them.

tldr.problem: Mail servers enforce limits such as a cap on recipients per transaction, but clients only learn about them by exceeding them and getting temporary or permanent errors, which causes delays or failed deliveries.
tldr.mechanism: The server adds a LIMITS keyword to its EHLO (or LHLO) reply, followed by name=value pairs such as RCPTMAX=20, and the client adapts before sending anything. Limit names are kept in an IANA registry.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9422 defines three initial limits (MAILMAX, RCPTMAX, RCPTDOMAINMAX) and the registry for future ones. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Limit value syntax
facts.value: Six digits at most, "0" not allowed

today: RFC 9422 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2024, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It also notes that a few proposals for additional features were set aside for future work.

sections.title: Why Servers Need to Announce Limits
sections.content:
SMTP moves email messages between hosts, and each message can have one or more recipients. The Local Mail Transfer Protocol (LMTP) delivers messages to a system that has no mail queues of its own, and it also allows multiple messages with multiple recipients. Submission, the step where a user's mail program hands mail to a server, uses SMTP too.

To conserve resources and protect themselves from malicious clients, servers enforce limits, for example on the number of recipients in a single transaction. Servers may also change the limits depending on their assessment of a client's reputation. Because limits vary, clients can inadvertently exceed them, and the server answers with temporary (or sometimes permanent) errors. That can mean delays or even failed message transfer.

Servers have always been able to announce a limit in a reply, but the client has to issue a command first. The LIMITS extension announces limits before any substantive interaction, in the reply to EHLO (or LHLO for LMTP).
sections.eli5: Servers have rules, like a club with a guest limit. Before, you only found out about the rule when the bouncer turned you away. Now the bouncer tells you at the door.

sections.title: The LIMITS Keyword and Its Parameter
sections.content:
The extension is named LIMITS. A server that implements it lists LIMITS as a keyword in its reply to EHLO (LHLO in LMTP), and the keyword's parameter carries one or more limits, each with an optional value. The syntax, in ABNF, is a space-separated list of name or name=value items. A limit name is made of letters, digits, hyphens and underscores. A limit value is any visible character except the semicolon.

The extension adds no new SMTP commands and changes no existing command. A LIMITS parameter could, however, be attached to another SMTP extension that does those things.

All limits MUST be registered with IANA. On naming, limit names MUST be comprehensible but kept as short as possible, and common abbreviations such as MAX are encouraged. If a limit is tied to a particular command, its name SHOULD begin with that command's name, and names SHOULD end with terms describing the type of limit.
sections.eli5: The server writes its rules as a short list of labels and numbers, like "parcels=5". The labels have to be written the same way everywhere so every client can read them.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Must Behave
sections.content:
Several rules cover how the announced limits behave in practice.

  • Pipelining. A pipelining client sends a whole transaction without checking each response, so it cannot count successes versus failures. That is why RCPTMAX counts all RCPT TO commands, not just successful ones: counting the total is simple, while counting successes would stall the pipeline.
  • No in-session changes. The announcement is part of the reply to EHLO. Some servers vary limits as a session progresses, but this extension does not handle in-session changes.
  • SMTP minimums. SMTP requires servers to accept a minimum of 100 RCPT TO commands, but servers routinely impose smaller limits. There is no requirement that advertised limits comply with the SMTP minimums.
  • Repeated EHLO. The command must be reissued in some cases, such as after authentication or after negotiating a security layer. Servers MAY return updated limits then. Clients MUST discard previous limits in favor of the most recent EHLO, and if the newer reply has no limits, the client MUST act as if none were communicated.
  • Caching. Clients MAY cache limits for later sessions, but MUST be able to cope with any change between sessions.
sections.eli5: If the rules change halfway through, the newest announcement wins. You may remember the rules for next time, but you have to be ready for the club to change them.

sections.title: Handling Errors in the Parameter
sections.content:
Syntax errors in the basic parameter syntax are best handled by ignoring the value entirely, and clients SHOULD then proceed as if the LIMITS extension had not been used.

Syntax or other errors in the value of one specific limit, including unrecognized value keywords, are handled by ignoring just that limit. The client MUST proceed as if that limit had not been specified.

A future specification could create several interrelated limits. If so, it MUST say how an error in one limit's value affects the others.
sections.eli5: If one rule on the list is written in gibberish, you skip that rule and still follow the others. If the whole list is gibberish, you act as if there was no list.

sections.title: The Three Initial Limits
sections.content:
The RFC defines three limits. Each has the same value syntax: a number from 1 up, with a six-digit maximum, and "0" not allowed. None has restrictions, and each points to the Security Considerations.

  • MAILMAX is the maximum number of transactions (MAIL FROM commands) the server will accept in a single session. The count includes all MAIL FROM commands, whether they succeed or fail.
  • RCPTMAX is the maximum number of RCPT TO commands the server will accept in a single transaction. It is not a limit on actual recipients: one RCPT TO may produce several recipients or, on error, none.
  • RCPTDOMAINMAX is the maximum number of different domains that can appear in recipient addresses within a single session. Some servers impose it because they bind to a specific internal delivery mechanism on receipt of the first RCPT TO.
sections.eli5: There are three starter rules: how many separate parcels per visit, how many names on one parcel, and how many different towns the parcels can go to.

sections.title: Example Session
sections.content: In the RFC's example, the server answers EHLO example.org with a list of extensions that includes 250-LIMITS RCPTMAX=20 MAILMAX=5, alongside others such as SIZE 100000000, PIPELINING and STARTTLS. The client now knows to limit the number of recipients in a transaction to twenty and the number of transactions in a session to five.
sections.eli5: The server says "twenty names per parcel, five parcels per visit." The client keeps to that, so nothing gets turned away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists several risks. A malicious server can use limits to overly constrain client behavior, causing excessive use of client resources. A malicious client may use the advertised limits to optimize delivery of unwanted messages. A man-in-the-middle attack on unprotected SMTP connections can make clients misbehave, leading to delivery delays or failures and possibly a loss of reputation for the client.

The RFC adds that decades of operational experience with the SMTP SIZE extension indicate such abuse is rare and unlikely to be a significant problem. Using LIMITS to give client-specific information, as opposed to general server limits, unavoidably gives senders feedback about their reputation. Malicious senders can exploit this, for example by sending good email first and, once a reputation is established, sending bad email.
sections.eli5: Telling people the rules helps honest visitors, but a sneaky visitor can also use the rules to plan. And someone in the middle could tamper with the list of rules.

sections.title: The IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA has added LIMITS (description "Server limits") to the "SMTP Service Extensions" registry. It has also created an "SMTP Server Limits" registry in the "MAIL Parameters" group, with the policy "Specification Required", and registered the three limits from Section 4.

Each registry entry holds the limit's name, the syntax of its value (if it has one, with ABNF preferred but not required), a description of its semantics, any restrictions (including whether it is specific to SMTP, submission or LMTP), and security considerations. The Designated Expert(s) check that requests are consistent with the SMTP extension mechanisms and this specification.
sections.eli5: There is a public notebook where every official rule name gets written down, so everyone uses the same words for the same rule.
